newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST--US rates rise in Q4, ebb in 1997 - experts.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST--US rates rise in Q4, ebb in 1997 - experts.

text.p: U.S. long-term interest rates will rise through yearend and most of next year, but begin to ebb at the fourth quarter 1997 due to an eventual slowdown in the economy, according to a Reuters poll of U.S. economists.
On average, 33 experts surveyed on Monday forecast the 30-year Treasury bond yield would rise to 7.06 percent by yearend and hold nearby before dropping to 6.91 percent by October 1997.
Many experts calling for declining bond yields said the Federal Reserve would raise short-term interest rates in either November or December to keep potentially rising inflation at bay.

Any tightening by the Fed in the near future would relieve inflationary pressures and eventually slow Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth, said Paul Kasriel, chief U.S. economist at Northern Trust Co.
Kasriel said he sees the economy posting around 2.25 percent growth in the fourth quarter of this year and the first quarter of 1997. "That's what is generating the inflationary pressures."

Robert Brusca, chief economist at Nikko Securities Co International Inc, echoed those thoughts by asserting the economy is growing such that the Fed may have to slow it by tightening the federal funds rate by 50-basis points in November.
The Commerce Department last week reported a speedy final second-quarter GDP growth rate at 4.7 percent, up from 2.0 percent in the first quarter of 1996.
Despite the robust GDP figure, some economists envision a softer economy on the horizon.
"We're thinking the upcoming numbers are going to be reasonably soft," said Alan Ruskin, interantional economist at consulting firm I.D.E.A Inc.

Forecasting September non-farm payrolls to fall to 165,000, third-quarter GDP to fall to 2.0 percent and final sales to be below 2.0 percent, Ruskin said that is "an environment where the Fed is unlikely to tighten unless they see obvious signs of a pickup in inflation."
The shiftiness in the experts' sentiment is that the current economy is not infected with deep inflation psychology now, said Kasriel.
"It's not a boom. It's not a bust. The Fed is just fine-tuning this thing, making life extremely difficult for us forecasters," he said.
The experts predicted the two-year note yield would move in tandem with the long bond but not declining as much, leading to a flatter Treasury yield curve.
On average, the economists projected the two-year rate would rise as high as 6.41 percent by the second quarter 1997 and fall modestly to 6.32 percent by the fourth quarter.
Full results of the survey follow.
